posts.title: Understanding the Mortgage Appraisal Process for Homebuyers
posts.excerpt: When you finance a home purchase, the appraisal helps your lender evaluate the collateral for your loan. Here is how the mortgage appraisal process works, step by step.
posts.body_html:
Understanding the Mortgage Appraisal Process for Homebuyers

If you are financing a home purchase, the appraisal is one of the key steps between an accepted offer and closing. Your lender uses it to evaluate the property that will secure the loan, and the result can affect how much you can borrow and how the rest of the transaction unfolds.

This guide explains how the mortgage appraisal process works, what the appraiser does, how the appraised value affects your loan, and what your options are if the value comes in lower than expected.

Why Lenders Require an Appraisal

A mortgage is secured by the home you are buying. Before lending, the lender needs an independent opinion of the property's market value to understand the collateral behind the loan. The appraisal also documents the property's characteristics and condition, which helps the lender confirm that the home meets the requirements of the loan program.

Some loans qualify for an appraisal waiver or another valuation alternative, depending on the loan program and the lender's process. Your loan officer can tell you whether a full appraisal is required for your loan.

Who Orders the Appraisal — and Who Chooses the Appraiser

For a mortgage, the lender orders the appraisal, often through an appraisal management company. Appraiser independence rules are designed to keep the valuation impartial, so borrowers, real estate agents, and loan officers generally cannot select the appraiser or pressure the appraiser toward a particular value.

The borrower usually pays the appraisal fee, often at the start of the loan process. Fees vary with the property, the type of report, and the loan program; your lender will disclose the cost in your loan estimate.

Step by Step: How the Mortgage Appraisal Works

  1. The lender orders the appraisal after your loan application is underway and the purchase contract is in place.
  2. The appraiser schedules the inspection with the person who controls access to the home — typically the seller or the listing agent for a purchase.
  3. The appraiser inspects the property, observing the interior and exterior, noting features, updates, and condition, measuring the home, and taking photographs.
  4. The appraiser researches the market, including recent sales of comparable homes, active and pending listings, and market trends.
  5. The appraiser analyzes the data and writes the report, applying the valuation approaches that fit the property and reconciling them into an opinion of market value.
  6. The lender reviews the report as part of underwriting.

Timing varies with the property, the market, and the lender's process. If your contract has an appraisal-related deadline, make sure your lender and agent know it at the start.

How the Appraised Value Affects Your Loan

Lenders typically base the maximum loan amount on the property's value. For a purchase, that is generally the lower of the purchase price or the appraised value, combined with the maximum loan-to-value ratio allowed by your loan program.

Here is a simplified example. Suppose you agree to buy a home for $400,000 and plan to borrow 90 percent:

ScenarioValue used by lender90% loanCash needed beyond the loan
Appraisal at $400,000$400,000$360,000$40,000
Appraisal at $390,000$390,000$351,000$49,000

In the second scenario, the price did not change, but the loan amount did — so the buyer would need to bring more cash, renegotiate, or consider other options. (This example omits closing costs and assumes the program allows 90 percent financing.)

Condition and "subject to" appraisals

If the appraiser observes issues that affect safety, soundness, or the loan program's property requirements, the appraisal may be completed "subject to" specific repairs or completion of work. In that case, the lender may require the work to be finished and inspected before closing, sometimes with a brief follow-up inspection by the appraiser.

What If the Appraisal Comes in Low?

A value below the contract price is sometimes called an "appraisal gap." Common options include:

  • Renegotiating the price with the seller
  • Covering the difference in cash
  • Restructuring the financing, if your loan program allows
  • Terminating the contract, if your contract and any addenda give you that right

In Texas, whether you can terminate — and by when — depends on the terms of your purchase contract and any financing or appraisal addenda. Your real estate agent or attorney can explain your specific rights.

Requesting a reconsideration of value

If you believe the report contains factual errors — for example, the wrong square footage or bedroom count — or overlooked relevant comparable sales, ask your lender about its reconsideration of value (ROV) process. Requests go through the lender, not directly to the appraiser, and the most effective ones are specific and supported by data available as of the appraisal's effective date.

You Are Entitled to a Copy

Federal rules generally require your lender to give you a copy of the appraisal promptly, and no later than three business days before closing unless you have waived that timing. Read it carefully: our guide on how to read an appraisal report walks through each section.

How the Seller Can Help the Inspection Go Smoothly

For a purchase, the seller usually controls the property during the appraisal. Practical steps include providing access to every room, the attic, the garage, and mechanical equipment; keeping pets secured; and preparing a list of significant improvements with approximate dates. Cleaning and decluttering make the inspection easier but do not by themselves change market value. Learn more in What Is a Home Appraisal and Why Does It Matter?

Appraisals Outside the Mortgage Process

Not every appraisal is ordered by a lender. Homeowners, sellers, attorneys, and executors can engage an appraiser directly for purposes such as a pre-purchase appraisal, a pre-listing appraisal, or PMI removal.

posts.title: How to Read Your Appraisal Report: A Clear Guide
posts.excerpt: An appraisal report shows not just a value, but how the appraiser got there. This guide walks through each major section so you can read your report with confidence.
posts.body_html:
How to Read Your Appraisal Report: A Clear Guide

An appraisal report does more than state a number. A credible report explains what was appraised, which market data the appraiser relied on, how that data was analyzed, and why the final opinion of value is supported. Knowing where to look makes the report far easier to understand — whether you are a homeowner, buyer, seller, attorney, or real estate professional.

This guide walks through the major sections found in most residential appraisal reports. If you are new to appraisals, you may want to start with what a home appraisal is and why it matters.

First, Note the Report Type

Most mortgage appraisals for single-family homes are prepared on the Uniform Residential Appraisal Report (URAR), a standardized form used for loans sold to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. Those agencies are transitioning to a redesigned URAR under an updated Uniform Appraisal Dataset (UAD 3.6), so the layout of your report may differ from older examples you find online. Appraisals for private purposes — such as divorce, estate, or pre-listing assignments — may use a different format.

Whatever the format, every appraisal report prepared under the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice (USPAP) must identify the client, the intended use, the type and definition of value, the effective date, and the scope of work. Read these first: they tell you what question the appraisal answers.

The Subject Property Section

This section describes the property being appraised — the "subject." Look for:

  • Identification: address, legal description, and parcel number
  • Site: lot size, zoning, utilities, and any easements or adverse conditions noted
  • Improvements: year built, gross living area, room count, bedrooms, bathrooms, garage, and notable features
  • Condition and quality: the appraiser's observations about maintenance, updates, and construction quality

Check the facts carefully. If the square footage, bedroom count, or a major feature is wrong, that is the kind of factual error worth raising with the party who ordered the appraisal.

Condition and quality ratings

Many lender reports express condition and quality using standardized ratings — for example, C1 through C6 for condition, where lower numbers indicate better condition. The report should describe the observations that support the rating, such as the age of kitchen and bathroom updates or deferred maintenance.

The Neighborhood and Market Conditions

This part of the report describes the area around the subject property and the direction of the market: whether values are increasing, stable, or declining; how supply compares with demand; and typical marketing times. These conditions matter because an appraisal reflects the market as of a specific effective date.

The Sales Comparison Approach and Adjustment Grid

For most homes, this is the heart of the report. The appraiser selects recent sales of similar homes — the "comparables" or "comps" — and presents them side by side with the subject property in an adjustment grid.

How to read the grid:

  1. Compare the basics. Look at location, distance from the subject, sale date, size, age, and condition. Good comparables are as similar as the market allows.
  2. Read the adjustments. When a comparable is superior to the subject in some respect, the appraiser makes a downward adjustment to its sale price; when it is inferior, the adjustment is upward. The goal is to estimate what each comparable would have sold for if it were more like the subject.
  3. Review the adjusted sale prices. After adjustments, the comparables should point to a reasonably consistent range of value.
  4. Read the commentary. The appraiser should explain why particular sales were chosen and how significant adjustments were supported.

A reasonable question to ask is not "Is there a higher sale nearby?" but "Is this comparable truly similar, and was it available to the appraiser as of the effective date?"

The Cost and Income Approaches

Depending on the property and assignment, the report may also include:

  • The cost approach: estimated land value plus the cost to construct the improvements new, less depreciation. It is often given more weight for newer or unique homes.
  • The income approach: a value indication based on rental income, most relevant for rental and multi-unit properties.

If an approach was not developed, the report should explain why.

Reconciliation and the Final Opinion of Value

In reconciliation, the appraiser weighs the reliability of each approach and the quality of the data, then states a final opinion of value as of the effective date. Pay attention to:

  • The effective date — the date the value applies to, which can differ from the date the report was signed
  • Conditions or assumptions — for example, a value "subject to" completion of repairs, or an extraordinary assumption
  • The certification — the appraiser's signed statements of impartiality and compliance with USPAP

How Long Is an Appraisal Valid?

An appraisal states value as of its effective date; it does not expire on its own, but markets change. Lenders and loan programs set their own requirements for how recent an appraisal must be, and an older appraisal may require a market value update or recertification. For private purposes, a new appraisal is appropriate when market conditions or the property itself have changed.

What If You Disagree With the Report?

For a mortgage appraisal, communicate through your lender rather than contacting the appraiser directly. Many lenders have a formal reconsideration of value (ROV) process. The most useful requests are specific: factual errors in the property description, or relevant comparable sales that were available as of the effective date and are not discussed in the report.

For an appraisal you engaged privately, contact the appraiser with your questions. Keep in mind that an appraiser's fee cannot be contingent on reaching a particular value, and the appraiser must remain impartial.

Need a Professional Appraisal in Dallas–Fort Worth?

Our services include full residential appraisals, pre-listing appraisals, and divorce appraisals. We respond to appraisal requests within one business day.

posts.title: What Is a Home Appraisal and Why Does It Matter?
posts.excerpt: A home appraisal is an independent, professionally supported opinion of a property's market value. Here is what the process involves and why it matters for buyers, sellers, lenders, and homeowners.
posts.body_html:
What Is a Home Appraisal and Why Does It Matter?

A home appraisal is an independent, professionally supported opinion of a residential property's value as of a specific date. It is prepared by a state-licensed or certified appraiser who inspects or otherwise examines the property, researches the local market, and analyzes sales of comparable homes before reaching a conclusion.

Appraisals matter because many significant financial decisions rely on them: how much a lender will lend, whether a purchase price is supported, how marital property is divided, how an estate is settled, or whether a property tax assessment is reasonable. This article explains what an appraisal is, how the process works, and what homeowners can reasonably expect.

What a Home Appraisal Is — and What It Is Not

An appraisal is an opinion of value developed under professional standards. In the United States, appraisers follow the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice (USPAP), which require that the appraiser be impartial, have no undisclosed interest in the property, and support the conclusions in the report with credible analysis.

In most assignments, the appraiser develops an opinion of market value — broadly, the most probable price a property should bring in a competitive and open market, assuming a typically motivated buyer and seller who are both reasonably informed and acting in their own interests. The exact definition used depends on the assignment and the client.

An appraisal is not:

  • A home inspection. A home inspector evaluates the operation and condition of systems such as the roof, plumbing, and electrical. An appraiser observes condition as it relates to value but does not perform a home inspection.
  • A comparative market analysis (CMA). A real estate agent's CMA is a pricing estimate prepared to help list or buy a home. It is useful, but it is not prepared under USPAP by a licensed appraiser.
  • A tax assessment. County appraisal districts value properties in bulk for tax purposes using mass-appraisal methods, which can differ from an individual market value appraisal.

Who Prepares a Home Appraisal?

In Texas, real estate appraisers are licensed or certified by the Texas Appraiser Licensing and Certification Board (TALCB). Credential levels reflect required education, experience, and examinations, and they determine which types of properties and assignments an appraiser may complete.

American Appraisal Alliance's appraiser is a Texas Certified Residential Real Estate Appraiser — License No. 1324410-CR. American Appraisal Alliance has been providing professional real estate appraisal services since 1986.

Who orders the appraisal?

That depends on why the appraisal is needed:

  • Mortgage purchase or refinance: The lender orders the appraisal, often through an appraisal management company. Appraiser independence rules generally prevent borrowers, agents, and loan officers from selecting or influencing the appraiser.
  • Private purposes: Homeowners, attorneys, executors, and real estate professionals can engage an appraiser directly — for example, for a pre-listing appraisal, a divorce appraisal, an estate or date-of-death appraisal, a tax assessment appeal, or PMI removal.

How the Home Appraisal Process Works

While every assignment is different, a typical residential appraisal follows these steps:

  1. Defining the assignment. The appraiser confirms the client, intended use, type of value, effective date, and scope of work.
  2. Property inspection. For a full interior appraisal, the appraiser observes the interior and exterior, notes features, condition, and updates, measures the home, and takes photographs. Some assignments use an exterior-only inspection or a desktop appraisal instead.
  3. Market research. The appraiser studies recent sales, listings, and market trends in the subject property's area.
  4. Analysis. The appraiser selects comparable sales, makes adjustments for meaningful differences, and applies the valuation approaches that fit the property.
  5. Reconciliation and report. The appraiser reconciles the evidence into a final opinion of value and documents the support in a written report.

The time required for the inspection and for the finished report varies with the property's size and complexity, the type of report, and current demand. Your appraiser can give you an estimate when the assignment is discussed.

The Three Approaches to Value

Appraisers consider three recognized approaches and rely on those that are most applicable:

ApproachHow it worksWhen it carries the most weight
Sales comparisonCompares the property with similar homes that have sold, adjusting for differencesMost single-family homes in active markets
CostEstimates the cost to build the improvements new, subtracts depreciation, and adds land valueNew construction and unique properties
IncomeConverts the property's expected rental income into a value indicationRental and income-producing properties

For most owner-occupied homes in the Dallas–Fort Worth area, the sales comparison approach is the primary indicator of value. To see how these approaches appear in a finished report, read our guide on how to read an appraisal report.

What Influences an Appraised Value?

Appraised value reflects how the market responds to the property's characteristics, including:

  • Location: neighborhood, school district, access, and nearby influences
  • Size and layout: gross living area, bedroom and bathroom count, and functional utility
  • Condition and quality: maintenance, construction quality, and the age and quality of updates
  • Site features: lot size, view, and improvements such as pools or outbuildings
  • Market conditions: supply, demand, and price trends as of the effective date

Preparing for the inspection

Preparation helps the inspection go smoothly, but it is important to keep expectations accurate. Cleaning and decluttering make it easier for the appraiser to access and observe the home; they do not by themselves raise market value. What does help is information: a list of significant improvements with approximate dates and costs, permits for additions, and notes on any recent repairs. Make sure the appraiser can reach the attic, garage, mechanical areas, and every room.

Why a Home Appraisal Matters

  • Buyers gain independent support for the price they are paying.
  • Sellers can use a pre-listing appraisal to set an informed asking price.
  • Lenders rely on the appraisal to evaluate the collateral securing a loan.
  • Attorneys, executors, and homeowners use appraisals for divorce, estate settlement, and tax matters where an impartial, well-supported value is needed.

Request a Professional Appraisal

Request an appraisal online, call (469) 936-4240, or email orders@aaarea.net.

posts.body_html:
What Factors May Affect the Appraisal Value of a Property in Divorce Cases

By American Appraisal Alliance Editorial Team · Updated 2026-08-30

Fair market value, property condition, location, and comparable sales are among the primary factors that shape a residential appraisal prepared for a divorce or property-division matter. These appraisals should be developed in compliance with the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice (USPAP) and may be used by attorneys, parties, mediators, or courts as part of the property-division process. American Appraisal Alliance, serving the entire DFW Metroplex from Frisco, TX, prepares residential real estate appraisals for divorce and property-division matters throughout North Texas.

The value of a marital home in a divorce matter depends on an accurate, independent assessment of the property itself — not on either spouse's expectations or position in the case. Appraisers apply objective, well-supported methodologies to develop a credible, impartial opinion of value based on documented property conditions and current market data. This article addresses residential real estate valuation; personal property such as jewelry, art, antiques, or furnishings typically requires a separately qualified specialist in that category.

Key Takeaways

  • Property division in divorce often depends on an accurate understanding of what the marital home is worth; this article addresses valuation factors and is not legal advice.
  • American Appraisal Alliance prepares USPAP-compliant residential appraisals serving the entire DFW Metroplex across multiple Texas cities.
  • A professionally prepared, independent appraisal gives attorneys, parties, and courts a well-supported basis for property-division discussions.
  • Appraisers assess property condition, comparable sales, and market trends to develop a well-supported, impartial opinion of value for the marital home.

What Property Factors Drive Divorce Appraisal Value?

Multiple data points inform what a marital home is worth during a divorce matter, and appraisers weigh each one carefully. Appraisers may analyze information from sources such as MLS data, public records, builder information, and title-related records when relevant and available, along with other credible market data, to develop a well-supported opinion of current value for the property. Drawing on a range of credible, relevant data supports a well-documented valuation and helps reduce the likelihood of added scrutiny during the settlement process.

Local market conditions matter just as much as the physical property itself. Appraisers analyze relevant market data together with property-specific information — including characteristics such as lot size, condition, upgrades, and layout when relevant to the assignment — to determine how those factors affect value. A professionally developed appraisal can consider property-specific characteristics, relevant market evidence, assignment conditions, and documented analysis that an automated estimate may not fully address.

What makes dividing the family home so contentious?

Splitting shared assets ranks among the most emotionally charged and complex parts of any divorce. The family home can represent one of the largest assets on the table, and an inaccurate value can affect how spouses and their attorneys approach the division of remaining property and debt.

Does personal property need a separate appraisal too?

Yes. Fine art, antique furnishings, jewelry, and other collectibles typically require valuation by a professional appraiser qualified in that specific personal-property category. American Appraisal Alliance provides residential real estate appraisal services only and does not appraise personal property; divorcing spouses in North Texas with significant personal property should engage an appropriately qualified specialist for those items in addition to a real estate appraisal.

Why Does the Appraisal Date Affect Settlement Value?

Timing determines which market conditions apply to the marital home, and the effective date of value can materially affect the appraised figure — particularly in a shifting North Texas market. A property valued at the outset of divorce proceedings may carry a different figure than one valued closer to a hearing or settlement date. The appropriate effective date for a given assignment is typically determined by the client, the attorneys involved, court instructions, or the specific circumstances of the case; American Appraisal Alliance does not provide legal advice on which date should apply and defers to the client and legal counsel on that determination.

Appraisals prepared in accordance with USPAP follow a consistent, well-documented methodology regardless of when the assignment occurs. This consistency matters because family law cases often stretch across months, sometimes longer, with financial circumstances evolving throughout the process.

What happens if the market shifts between filing and finalization?

The appropriate response depends on the specific assignment. A follow-up appraisal service or update addressing a discrete element of a prior report — for example, confirming that repairs were completed — is not the same as a new current-market-value appraisal and should not automatically be treated as one. When circumstances call for an updated opinion of value reflecting current market conditions, a new appraisal, rather than a limited update, is typically the appropriate scope. Once the intended use, effective date, client requirements, and other assignment conditions have been established, American Appraisal Alliance can discuss appropriate appraisal-service options for a specific assignment; American Appraisal Alliance does not determine the legally required valuation date or the legal requirements of a divorce case, and defers to the client and legal counsel on those questions.

Does licensing affect appraisal timing?

Regulation through the Texas Appraiser Licensing & Certification Board applies regardless of when the report is ordered. That oversight supports consistent, objective appraisal practice, whether the assignment occurs early in proceedings or closer to settlement.

How May Appraisal Reports Be Used in Divorce Matters?

In many divorce and property-division matters, a professionally prepared appraisal from a licensed appraiser operating under USPAP — the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice — provides a documented, independent opinion of value that may be used or considered by attorneys, parties, mediators, or courts, in contrast to an automated online estimate, a current listing price, or a real estate agent's opinion of value. A jointly-owned home can represent one of the largest marital assets in a case, so a well-supported, independent valuation gives attorneys and the parties documented evidence to work from rather than guesswork. Whether a particular proceeding requires a specific type of valuation is a legal question best directed to qualified legal counsel.

Why does the type of appraisal matter in a divorce case?

A USPAP-compliant appraisal follows a defined assignment scope, relies on relevant market evidence, and documents its analysis and methodology, resulting in an independent, unbiased opinion of value. Automated estimates and informal opinions may not account for all property-specific characteristics and relevant market evidence that can be considered in a professionally developed appraisal. American Appraisal Alliance prepares residential appraisal reports intended to give attorneys, parties, and the court a well-supported basis for evaluating the marital home, though no appraiser can guarantee how a specific court or opposing party will respond to any report.

What does this mean for divorcing spouses in North Texas?

Well-documented residential appraisals may be used by divorcing spouses and family law attorneys across the DFW Metroplex — including Addison, Allen, Anna, Aubrey, Carrollton, and Coppell — as part of the property-division process, subject to the specific legal requirements of the case, on which American Appraisal Alliance does not advise. A well-prepared appraisal report typically provides:

  • A licensed, independent, and unbiased opinion of value tied to current market data
  • Clear documentation of the methodology and data supporting the value conclusion
  • A well-supported foundation attorneys and parties can reference during negotiations

Without a credible, professionally prepared valuation, property-division negotiations can become more difficult, and disputed values may need to be revisited later in the process.

FAQ

What Factors May Affect the Appraisal Value of a Property in Divorce Cases?

Appraisers weigh property condition, location, comparable sales, and current market data — drawing on sources such as MLS data, public records, builder information, and title-related records when relevant and available — to develop a well-supported opinion of value for the marital home.

Does personal property require a separate appraisal from the home?

Yes. Fine art, antique furnishings, jewelry, and other collectibles typically require valuation by a professional qualified in that specific personal-property category. American Appraisal Alliance provides residential real estate appraisal services only and does not appraise personal property.

Why does the appraisal date matter in a divorce settlement?

The effective date of an appraisal determines which market conditions apply to the valuation, which can affect the property's appraised value. The appropriate effective date for a given assignment is typically determined by the client, attorneys, or court instructions rather than by the appraiser, and American Appraisal Alliance does not provide legal advice on that determination.

Conclusion

Understanding the factors that influence property appraisal value is an important part of navigating a divorce settlement. An accurate, impartial valuation grounded in current market conditions, comparable sales data, and property-specific attributes gives both parties a well-supported, documented basis for property-division discussions. By engaging a certified appraiser who follows applicable professional standards and prepares well-documented, independent reports, divorcing spouses in North Texas can approach settlement negotiations with greater clarity and confidence.
